::: {.page-header-custom}
# Research

My research lies at the intersection of industrial organization, international trade, and macroeconomics. I study how firm-level behavior and market power shape welfare and aggregate outcomes.
:::

## Job Market Paper {#job-market-paper}

::: {.paper-list}
::: {.paper-item}
<span class="status">Draft in progress</span>

### Market Power and Firm-Level Welfare Incidence

<p class="authors">Sébastien Lamproye</p>

<p class="abstract">Which firms account for the welfare cost of market power? This paper develops a firm-level welfare-incidence measure for markup dispersion. The measure maps firm markups, size, sectoral demand curvature, and benchmark markups into the change in aggregate welfare generated by reducing an individual firm’s markup gap. I implement the framework using Belgian firm-level accounting data from 1980 to 2024.</p>

<div class="paper-links"><span>Draft will be updated before circulation</span></div>
:::
:::

## Working Papers

::: {.paper-list}
::: {.paper-item}
<span class="status">Working paper</span>

### Aggregating Markups in Production Networks

<p class="authors">with <a href="https://orbi.umons.ac.be/profile?uid=501113">Emmanuel Dhyne</a> (National Bank of Belgium and University of Mons)</p>

<p class="abstract">How should firm-level markups be aggregated when production takes place through input–output networks? We derive an aggregate markup consistent with household incidence and show how cost-based exposure weights trace distortions through the production network. We bring the framework to near-universe Belgian firm-to-firm data.</p>
:::

::: {.paper-item}
<span class="status">Working paper</span>

### Market Power and Firm-Level Welfare Impact in Production Networks

<p class="authors">with <a href="https://orbi.umons.ac.be/profile?uid=501113">Emmanuel Dhyne</a> (National Bank of Belgium and University of Mons)</p>

<p class="abstract">Which firms matter most for the welfare cost of market power in a production network? We map firm-level markups and firm-to-firm linkages into aggregate welfare losses and firm-level welfare effects, then implement the framework using Belgian administrative transaction data.</p>
:::

::: {.paper-item}
<span class="status">Working paper</span>

### When Comparison Makes Markets Tip

<p class="authors">with <a href="https://sites.google.com/view/phan-dda/welcome">Duy-Anh Phan</a> (Monash University)</p>

<p class="abstract">Transparency is usually thought to make markets more competitive by helping consumers compare alternatives. We show that in two-sided markets greater comparability can strengthen feedback across market sides, destabilize coexistence, and induce tipping toward a dominant platform.</p>
:::
:::

## Under Review

::: {.paper-list}
::: {.paper-item}
<span class="status">Under review</span>

### Technological Knowledge Intensity and Intergenerational Mobility across U.S. Regions

<p class="authors">Sébastien Lamproye</p>

<p class="abstract">This paper studies the regional relationship between technological knowledge intensity and intergenerational upward mobility in the United States. Combining mobility measures from the Opportunity Atlas with U.S. patent records, I document that regions with greater patent-based knowledge intensity exhibit higher upward mobility.</p>
:::
:::

### Are We More Accurate? Revisiting the European Commission’s Macroeconomic Forecasts

<p class="authors">with Andras Chabin and Milan Výškrabka</p>

<p class="abstract">This paper reassesses the accuracy of the European Commission’s macroeconomic forecasts and studies how forecast performance has evolved over time.</p>

### Contracts, Corruption, and Relocation: A Theory of Carbon Leakage

<p class="authors">with <a href="https://sites.google.com/view/phan-dda/welcome">Duy-Anh Phan</a> (Monash University)</p>

<p class="abstract">A theory of environmental regulation with delegated enforcement, corruption, and firm mobility. The project studies how institutional asymmetries can generate pollution-haven forces even when formal abatement rules are identical.</p>
